parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Define activity of a radioactive sample.

markscheme_points.text: number of nuclear disintegrations per unit time

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is actually happening in the sample - nuclei are breaking up spontaneously, so what quantity counted per second tells you how active the sample is?
parts.proper_answer: Activity is the number of nuclear disintegrations per unit time, measured in $\text{Bq}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Activity Means Physically**
Imagine sitting beside the sample with a detector. Every time an unstable nucleus decays, you get one count. Activity tells you how many of those decay events happen each second. It is a rate, so its unit is $\text{s}^{-1}$, given the special name becquerel, $\text{Bq}$.

Step 2: **Precise Definition**
So you can state it simply as: $$A = -\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta t}$$ in words, the number of nuclear disintegrations per unit time.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain why the variation with time of the activity of a radioactive sample is exponential in nature.

markscheme_points.text: activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei
activity = (–) rate of change of number of undecayed nuclei
N is proportional to the rate of change of N (so exponential variation)

hints: Hint 1: Start from the nuclei themselves - with fewer undecayed nuclei left, would you expect more decays per second or fewer?
Hint 2: Link activity to how fast $N$ is decreasing, remembering that each decay removes one undecayed nucleus.
Hint 3: Recall what type of mathematical behaviour results when the rate of loss of a quantity is proportional to the amount still present.
parts.proper_answer: Activity $A$ is proportional to the number $N$ of undecayed nuclei present, $A = \lambda N$. Activity is the rate of decrease of $N$, $A = -dN/dt$. Hence rate of change of $N$ is proportional to $N$, which gives exponential decay of $N$ and of $A$ with time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Activity Depends on How Many Nuclei Are Left**
Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random, but each nucleus has the same chance of decaying per second. That chance is $\lambda$. With $N$ undecayed nuclei present, the total decays per second is: $$A = \lambda N$$ So when $N$ is large, activity is large. When $N$ falls, activity falls in proportion.

Step 2: **Activity Is the Rate of Loss of N**
Every disintegration removes one undecayed nucleus, so activity is also how fast $N$ is decreasing: $$A = -\frac{dN}{dt}$$ The minus sign just shows $N$ is getting smaller.

Step 3: **Why This Gives an Exponential**
Put the two ideas together: $$-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$$ The rate of change of $N$ is proportional to $N$ itself. Whenever that happens in physics, the solution is exponential: $$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$ and since $A = \lambda N$, activity follows the same shape: $$A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$ That is why the variation is exponential.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A sample contains a single radioactive isotope that decays to form a stable isotope.

The sample has an activity of $180\text{ Bq}$ at time $t = 0$.
At a time $8.4$ minutes later, the activity is $120\text{ Bq}$.
parts.text: Determine the decay constant, in $\text{min}^{-1}$, of the radioactive isotope.
hints: Hint 1: List what you know at $t = 0$ and at $t = 8.4\text{ min}$ - you have an initial activity and a later, smaller activity, with time kept in minutes throughout.
Hint 2: Apply $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ with your values and take natural logs to isolate $\lambda$.
parts.proper_answer: $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ gives $120 = 180 e^{-\lambda \times 8.4}$, so $\lambda = 0.048\text{ min}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set Up the Decay Law**
Activity follows the same exponential as $N$. With $A_0 = 180\text{ Bq}$ at $t = 0$ and $A = 120\text{ Bq}$ at $t = 8.4\text{ min}$: $$A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$ $$120 = 180 e^{-\lambda \times 8.4}$$ Keep time in minutes so $\lambda$ comes out in $\text{min}^{-1}$ directly.

Step 2: **Solve for the Decay Constant**
Divide and take natural logs: $$\frac{120}{180} = e^{-8.4\lambda}$$ $$\ln\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = -8.4\lambda$$ $$\lambda = -\frac{\ln(2/3)}{8.4} = 0.048\text{ min}^{-1}$$ to two significant figures.

Hint 2: Apply $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ with your values and take natural logs to isolate $\lambda$.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Use your answer in (c)(i) to determine the half-life, in $\text{min}$, of the radioactive isotope.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the meaning of half-life - the time for activity to fall to half - and how it is linked to the $\lambda$ value you have just calculated using natural log of 2.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From Decay Constant to Half-Life**
Half-life is the time for $A$ to become $A_0/2$. Putting that into the exponential gives the standard link: $$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$ Using $\lambda = 0.048\text{ min}^{-1}$: $$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{0.048} = 14\text{ min}$$

parts.label: (c)(iii)

markscheme_points.text: line with negative gradient throughout, starting at (0, 180)
curve with negative gradient passing through (8.4, 120)
curve with decreasing negative gradient, from t = 0 to t = 24 min, passing through (14, 90)

hints: Hint 1: Think about the starting point on the $A$-axis and the overall shape - does activity drop at a steady rate or drop fast at first then more slowly?
Hint 2: Mark the two fixed data points you know - the start value and the value at $t = 8.4\text{ min}$ - that your smooth curve must pass through.
Hint 3: Use your half-life to locate where activity is exactly half the starting value, then continue halving to $t = 24\text{ min}$ to guide the curve.
parts.proper_answer: Smooth exponential curve from $(0, 180\text{ Bq})$ through $(8.4\text{ min}, 120\text{ Bq})$ and $(14\text{ min}, 90\text{ Bq})$, with negative gradient of decreasing magnitude to $t = 24\text{ min}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start and Shape**
Begin at $A = 180\text{ Bq}$ when $t = 0$. The curve must fall with a negative gradient throughout, but it is not a straight line. It is steepest at the start when activity is highest, then flattens as activity falls - the gradient magnitude keeps decreasing.

Step 2: **Fix Key Points**
Draw a smooth curve passing through $(8.4\text{ min}, 120\text{ Bq})$ from the data. Then use the half-life of $14\text{ min}$: at $t = 14\text{ min}$, $A = 90\text{ Bq}$, exactly half of $180\text{ Bq}$. That is a very useful check point.

Step 3: **Extend to 24 min**
Continue the smooth flattening curve to $t = 24\text{ min}$. You can check further: after about two half-lives ($28\text{ min}$) activity would be near $45\text{ Bq}$, so at $24\text{ min}$ expect roughly $55\text{ Bq}$. Never let the curve become straight, level off to zero early, or increase.
